paragraphs.heading: What makes a bird
paragraphs.text: Birds are vertebrate animals belonging to the class Aves. They are marked by feathers, beaked jaws without teeth, hard-shelled eggs, a high metabolic rate, a heart with four chambers and a skeleton that is strong but light. They are warm-blooded and live all over the world. More than 11,000 living species exist, sorted into 44 orders, and over half of them are passerines, the perching birds.

paragraphs.heading: Size and wings
paragraphs.text: Sizes run from the 5.5 cm bee hummingbird to the 2.8 m common ostrich. Nearly every bird has wings, which are modified forelimbs, and how they develop varies with the way each species lives. Wings gave birds flight, but some later lost it, including ratites, penguins and many species found only on particular islands. The extinct moa and elephant birds are the only known groups with no wings at all. Bird digestive and breathing systems are adapted for flight, and some seabirds and waterbirds have also evolved for swimming.

paragraphs.heading: Living dinosaurs
paragraphs.text: Birds evolved from earlier theropods, so they are the only dinosaurs still alive. Their closest living relatives are the crocodilians, and together the two form a group called the archosaurs. Birds descend from early avialans, a group that includes Archaeopteryx and first appeared in the Late Jurassic. Some estimates place the rise of modern birds in the Cretaceous, with a burst of new forms around the extinction event 66 million years ago that wiped out the pterosaurs and all non-ornithuran dinosaurs.

paragraphs.heading: Reptiles or a class of their own
paragraphs.text: Traditional Linnaean classification gave birds a class of their own, owing to their unusual body plan and because, apart from mammals, they are the only animal group in which every species is warm-blooded. In the modern cladistic sense, though, birds count as reptiles. Modern phylogenetic taxonomy places Aves inside the theropods, sometimes at a rank below class. Birds and crocodilians are the only living members of the reptile group Archosauria.

paragraphs.heading: Social lives
paragraphs.text: Birds are social. They communicate with visual signals, calls and songs, and they breed and hunt together, flock, and mob predators; many social species pass knowledge down the generations, which is a form of culture. Most species are socially monogamous, though not necessarily sexually so, usually for one breeding season, sometimes for years and rarely for life. Others have one male with many females or, rarely, one female with many males. Eggs are fertilised by sexual reproduction and usually laid in a nest, where the parents incubate them. Most chicks get a long period of parental care after hatching.

paragraphs.heading: Birds and people
paragraphs.text: The study of birds is called ornithology. Francis Willughby and John Ray produced the first bird classification in their 1676 book Ornithologiae, and Carl Linnaeus reworked it in 1758 into the system still in use. Birds supply people with eggs, meat and feathers; songbirds and parrots are kept as pets; and guano, which is bird droppings, is gathered as fertiliser. Birdwatching is an important part of ecotourism. Yet human activity has driven about 120 to 130 species extinct since the 17th century and threatens about 1,200 bird species with extinction.
